claim: New SARS-CoV-2 variants, breakthrough infections, waning immunity, and sub-optimal vaccination rates account for surges of hospitalizations and deaths.
source: New SARS-CoV-2 variants, breakthrough infections, waning immunity, and sub-optimal vaccination rates account for surges of hospitalizations and deaths.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established knowledge about COVID-19 pandemic dynamics.

claim: CODOP was trained, tested and validated with six cohorts encompassing 29223 COVID-19 patients from more than 150 hospitals in Spain, the USA and Latin America during 2020–22.
source: CODOP was trained, tested and validated with six cohorts encompassing 29223 COVID-19 patients from more than 150 hospitals in Spain, the USA and Latin America during 2020–22.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the study's data collection and methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: CODOP uses 12 clinical parameters commonly measured at hospital admission for reaching high discriminative ability up to 9 days before clinical resolution (AUROC: 0·90–0·96).
source: CODOP uses 12 clinical parameters commonly measured at hospital admission for reaching high discriminative ability up to 9 days before clinical resolution (AUROC: 0·90–0·96)
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript, including specific AUROC values.

claim: CODOP maintains its predictive ability independently of the virus variant and the vaccination status.
source: Furthermore, CODOP maintains its predictive ability independently of the virus variant and the vaccination status.
evidence: This claim is supported by testing CODOP on cohorts with different variants and vaccination statuses as described in the results.

claim: CODOP calculators validated with a cohort of patients from 42 hospitals in three Latin American countries achieved 78–100% sensitivity and 89–97% specificity.
source: validated with a cohort of patients from 42 hospitals in three Latin American countries (78–100% sensitivity and 89–97% specificity).
evidence: This claim is supported by the external validation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated the pandemic as the direct cause of more than six million deaths.
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated the pandemic as the direct cause of more than six million deaths.
evidence: This claim references WHO data, which is a citation to an external authoritative source.

claim: Viral variants carry a higher risk of hospitalization.
source: The appearance of viral variants that are more contagious and that carry a higher risk of hospitalization, (Twohig et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Twohig et al., 2022.

claim: A vaccine-alone exit strategy will likely not be sufficient to contain further outbreaks and their consequences.
source: support recent models showing that a vaccine-alone exit strategy will likely not be sufficient to contain further outbreaks and their consequences (Moore et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moore et al., 2021.

claim: Numerous models have been developed to assist in triage decisions of hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
source: Thus, numerous models have been developed to assist in triage decisions of hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the field.

claim: Independent evaluations have pointed out the lack of generalizability and limited clinical use of existing COVID-19 prediction models.
source: However, independent evaluations have pointed out their lack of generalizability and their limited clinical use (Wynants et al., 2020; El-Solh et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wynants et al., 2020 and El-Solh et al., 2020.

claim: COVID-19 has more than 60 disease subtypes.
source: Moreover, the heterogeneity of the host-pathogen interaction (what results in more than 60 disease subtypes of COVID-19 DeMerle et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DeMerle et al., 2021.

claim: The training cohort is based on the SEMI COVID-19 Registry.
source: The training and two test cohorts (Test 1 and Test 2) of this study are based on the SEMI (Sociedad Espanola de Medicina Interna) COVID-19 Registry (Casas-Rojo et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Casas-Rojo et al., 2020.

claim: The SEMI COVID-19 Registry is an ongoing multicentre nationwide cohort of consecutive patients hospitalized for COVID-19 across 109 hospitals in different Spanish regions.
source: It is an ongoing multicentre nationwide cohort of consecutive patients hospitalized for COVID-19 across different Spanish regions (109 hospitals).
evidence: This claim describes the data source used in the study.

claim: Eligibility criteria included age ≥18 years, confirmed diagnosis of COVID-19, first hospital admission for COVID-19, and hospital discharge or in-hospital death.
source: Eligibility criteria were age ≥18 years, confirmed diagnosis of COVID-19, defined as a positive result on real-time reverse-transcription-polymerase-chain-reaction (RT-PCR) for the presence of SARS-CoV-2 in nasopharyngeal swab specimens or sputum samples, first hospital admission for COVID-19, and hospital discharge or in-hospital death (Casas-Rojo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim describes the study's inclusion criteria and is supported by citation.

claim: Test 4 cohort was composed of 2508 patients hospitalized in the 12 de Octubre and the Costa del Sol Spanish hospitals.
source: An additional patient cohort (named Test 4 and composed of 2508 patients hospitalized in the 12 de Octubre and the Costa del Sol Spanish hospitals), was used for testing the influence of vaccination and the Delta and Omicron virus variants on the discriminative ability of CODOP for predicting in-hospital death, the need for mechanical ventilation and admission to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).
evidence: This claim describes the composition of Test 4 cohort.

claim: The test cohort from New York consisted of 2021 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in the Mount Sinai Health System in New York City.
source: The test cohort from New York (External Test 3) is based on the study from Del Valle et al., 2020 consisting of 2 021 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in the Mount Sinai Health System in New York City.
evidence: This claim describes the External Test 3 cohort and is supported by citation.

claim: The online validation cohorts were provided by 42 hospitals from Argentina, Honduras, and Bolivia.
source: The cohorts used in the online validation of the two online CODOP subtypes were provided by a group of Argentinian hospitals composed by the Argentinian COVID-19 Network (4690 patients from 37 Argentinian hospitals), Hospital Vélez Sarsfield (100 patients, Buenos Aires, Argentina), and Hospital Británico de Buenos Aires (150 patients, Buenos Aires, Argentina), the Honduras Medical Centre (45 patients, Tegucigalpa, Honduras), the Hospital Santa Cruz Caja Petrolera de Salud (30 patients, Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia), and the Hospital San Juan de Dios (93 patients, Santa Cruz, Bolivia).
evidence: This claim describes the online validation cohorts.

claim: CODOP was developed using modified stable iterative variable selection (SIVS) and linear regression with lasso regularisation.
source: CODOP was built using modified stable iterative variable selection (SIVS) (Mahmoudian et al., 2021) and linear regression with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (lasso) regularisation (Friedman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology and is supported by citations.

claim: In model building only the training cohort was used and models were built using 10-fold cross-validation.
source: In model building only the training cohort was used and models were built using 10-fold cross-validation.
evidence: This claim describes the model development methodology.

claim: CODOP uses 11 blood biochemical parameters plus Age.
source: Using linear Lasso, 10-fold cross-validation and SIVS, we obtained a final CODOP model using 11 blood biochemical parameters plus Age (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model development results.

claim: Elevated values of Age, neutrophils, C-reactive protein, creatinine, lactate dehydrogenase, serum sodium, serum potassium, glucose and D-dimer were positively correlated with in-hospital death.
source: Detailed analysis indicated elevated values of Age, neutrophils, C-reactive protein, creatinine, lactate dehydrogenase, serum sodium, serum potassium, glucose and D-dimer, and reduced values of platelets, eosinophils and monocytes were positively correlated with in-hospital death, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the model features.

claim: Reduced values of platelets, eosinophils and monocytes were positively correlated with in-hospital death.
source: Detailed analysis indicated elevated values of Age, neutrophils, C-reactive protein, creatinine, lactate dehydrogenase, serum sodium, serum potassium, glucose and D-dimer, and reduced values of platelets, eosinophils and monocytes were positively correlated with in-hospital death, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the model features.

claim: CODOP showed a superior discriminative ability in predicting in-hospital mortality (AUROC: 0·889, 95% CI 0·885–0·894) compared to benchmarked predictors.
source: CODOP showed a superior discriminative ability in predicting in-hospital mortality (area under the receiver operating curves or AUROC: 0·889, 95% CI 0·885–0·894; Figure 2A) reaching 0·84% and 0·78% sensitivity and specificity, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the benchmarking results and Figure 2A.

claim: CODOP reached 0·84% sensitivity and 0·78% specificity in the training cohort.
source: CODOP showed a superior discriminative ability in predicting in-hospital mortality (area under the receiver operating curves or AUROC: 0·889, 95% CI 0·885–0·894; Figure 2A) reaching 0·84% and 0·78% sensitivity and specificity, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the performance metrics in the training cohort.

claim: CODOP has better calibration for all the different risk groups as reflected by a lower RMSE value compared to benchmarked predictors.
source: In addition, CODOP has better calibration for all the different risk groups as reflected by a lower RMSE value (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the calibration analysis and Figure 2B.

claim: The predictor published by Zhang et al. underestimated the probability of death for low-risk patients and overestimates the probability of death for high-risk patients.
source: A detailed inspection of the calibration curves shows that the predictor published by Zhang et al. underestimated the probability of death for low-risk patients and overestimates the probability of death for high-risk patients.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of calibration curves comparing CODOP to Zhang et al.'s predictor.

claim: COPE underestimates the probability of death for all risk groups.
source: On the other side, while COPE underestimates the probability of death for all risk groups, Age showed a clear overestimation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of calibration curves.

claim: Age showed a clear overestimation of the probability of death.
source: On the other side, while COPE underestimates the probability of death for all risk groups, Age showed a clear overestimation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of calibration curves.

claim: Test 1 cohort consisted of 3118 COVID-19 patients hospitalized during consecutive COVID-19 waves that occurred in Spain between July 7th and December 6th 2020.
source: On the one side, we used two time-sliced cohorts with COVID-19 patients hospitalized during consecutive COVID-19 waves that occurred in Spain between July 7th and December 6th 2020 (Test 1; 3118 patients)
evidence: This claim describes the Test 1 cohort composition.

claim: Test 2 cohort consisted of 566 patients hospitalized between December 7th 2020 and March 31st 2021.
source: between December 7th 2020 and March 31st 2021 (Test 2; 566 patients).
evidence: This claim describes the Test 2 cohort composition.

claim: Test 1 and Test 2 cohorts are composed of non-vaccinated patients infected with the original Wuhan and the Alpha virus variants.
source: These cohorts are composed of non-vaccinated patients infected with the original Wuhan and the Alpha virus variants.
evidence: This claim describes the characteristics of Test 1 and Test 2 cohorts.

claim: The performance metrics of CODOP are preserved in Test 1 and Test 2 cohorts.
source: ROC and calibration curves show that the performance metrics are preserved in these two cohorts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ROC and calibration curves in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The generalizability of CODOP was demonstrated on External Test 3 consisting of 2021 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in the Mount Sinai Health System in New York City between March 21st and April 28th, 2020.
source: The generalizability of CODOP was also demonstrated on a separate test cohort (External Test (3) consisting of 2021 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in the Mount Sinai Health System in New York City between March 21st and April 28th, 2020 Del Valle et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the results on External Test 3 and citation.

claim: Test 4 dataset was collected in Spain between April 1st 2021 and February 27th 2022.
source: To investigate the influence of the Delta and Omicron VOCs, we analysed a dataset collected in Spain between April 1st 2021 and February 27th 2022 (Test 4; 2508 patients).
evidence: This claim describes the Test 4 cohort.

claim: The performance of CODOP is preserved when Delta and Omicron VOCs were dominant.
source: Our data demonstrate that the performance of CODOP is preserved when these two types of VOC were dominant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of Test 4 cohort.

claim: CODOP has the same discriminative ability in patients infected by Delta or by Omicron.
source: A detailed analysis shows that CODOP has the same discriminative ability in patients infected by Delta or by Omicron (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is no correlation between the percentage of deaths and the predictive ability of CODOP among the four test cohorts.
source: The lack of correlation between the percentage of deaths and the predictive ability of CODOP among the four test cohorts (Supplementary file 1), rules out an artefactual influence due to the time-sliced nature of these cohorts.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the relationship between death rates and CODOP performance.

claim: CODOP overperformed both the benchmarked predictors and Age in the test cohorts.
source: Finally, CODOP overperformed both the benchmarked predictors and Age in the test cohorts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the benchmarking results in the test cohorts.

claim: Vaccination status has little influence on the ability of CODOP for predicting the risk of in-hospital death.
source: Our data show that vaccination status has little influence on the ability of CODOP for predicting the risk of in-hospital death (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of vaccinated patients in Test 4 cohort.

claim: CODOP captures key biomarkers involved in the physiological deterioration of COVID-19 hospitalized patients.
source: Altogether, our results show the stability of CODOP during the fluctuating scenario of the COVID-19 pandemic (the appearance of different VOCs, the different immune protection among the population, the use of more tailored clinical interventions), suggesting that CODOP captures key biomarkers involved in the physiological deterioration of COVID-19 hospitalized patients.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the stability of CODOP across different scenarios.

claim: CODOP predicted the outcome of all patients nine days in advance with an average sensitivity higher than 90% (at a fixed specificity of 75%).
source: On average, CODOP predicted the outcome of all patients nine days in advance with an average sensitivity (at a fixed specificity of 75%) and AUROC values higher than 90% (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by the horizon analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CODOP predicted the outcome of all patients nine days in advance with AUROC values higher than 90%.
source: On average, CODOP predicted the outcome of all patients nine days in advance with an average sensitivity (at a fixed specificity of 75%) and AUROC values higher than 90% (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by the horizon analysis results.

claim: CODOP maintained a stable sensitivity along the nine days horizon time significantly outperforming other benchmarked predictors (p < 0.01, paired two-sided T-test).
source: In comparison to the other benchmarked predictors, CODOP maintained a stable sensitivity along the nine days horizon time significantly outperforming (Figure 3A; p < 0.01, paired two-sided T-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CODOP enables a continuous stratification of patients into a high-risk group over the course of the hospitalization.
source: Next, we demonstrated that CODOP enables a continuous stratification of patients into a high-risk group over the course of the hospitalization, as patients with a higher risk score (which refers to the probability provided by CODOP), who were more likely to die over time (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the survival analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Patients with a higher CODOP risk score were more likely to die over time.
source: as patients with a higher risk score (which refers to the probability provided by CODOP), who were more likely to die over time (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the survival analysis.

claim: CODOP represents an early and dynamic warning tool in the clinical status of COVID-19 patients.
source: Hence, CODOP represents an early and dynamic warning tool in the clinical status of COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the horizon and survival analyses.

claim: CODOP-Ovt maximizes the negative predictive value or the detection of high-risk patients (high sensitivity).
source: CODOP-Ovt maximizes the negative predictive value or the detection of high-risk patients (high sensitivity) and it is meant for scenarios where overtriage is possible because hospital resources are not the main limitation.
evidence: This claim describes the design and purpose of CODOP-Ovt.

claim: CODOP-Unt maximizes the positive predictive value by trying to avoid the inclusion of false high-risk patients (high specificity).
source: On the other side, CODOP-Unt maximizes the positive predictive value by trying to avoid the inclusion of false high-risk patients (high specificity) and it might be preferred in pandemic conditions when hospital resources are limited and undertriage needs to be considered.
evidence: This claim describes the design and purpose of CODOP-Unt.

claim: CODOP-Ovt identified >95% of the patients that finally died in hospital nine days before clinical resolution.
source: Using the initial training cohort, CODOP-Ovt identified >95% of the patients that finally died in hospital nine days before clinical resolution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of CODOP-Ovt shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase in sensitivity of CODOP-Ovt is concomitant with reduced specificity (60%–70%).
source: As expected, this increase in sensitivity is concomitant with reduced specificity (60%–70%; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the performance metrics of CODOP-Ovt.

claim: The metrics of CODOP-Ovt are within the range of recommended under- and overtriage levels ranging from 5% to 10% and 25% to 50%, respectively.
source: Notably, these metrics are within the range of recommended under- and overtriage levels ranging from 5% to 10% and 25% to 50%, respectively (van Rein et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim compares CODOP metrics to established guidelines and is supported by citation.

claim: CODOP-Unt correctly predicted more than 95% of the patients that survived as low-risk.
source: The opposite results were obtained with CODOP-Unt, where more than 95% of the patients that survived were correctly predicted as low-risk (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of CODOP-Unt.

claim: CODOP-Unt missed 40%–50% of the patients that died in hospital.
source: while 40%–50% of the patients that died in hospital were not detected in advance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of CODOP-Unt.

claim: Confusion matrixes show similar overall performance for both CODOP subtypes in all test cohorts.
source: Confusion matrixes show similar overall performance for both CODOP subtypes in all test cohorts (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the confusion matrix analysis.

claim: A web-based application for CODOP was constructed and evaluated at https://gomezvarelalab.em.mpg.de/codop/.
source: Following this, we constructed and evaluated an easy-to-use web-based application (https://gomezvarelalab.em.mpg.de/codop/) that offers the possibility to choose between CODOP-Ovt and CODOP-Unt.
evidence: This claim describes the development of the web application.

claim: The web application has been tested using different devices, web browsers and operative systems.
source: The web application has been tested using different devices, web browsers and operative systems (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim describes the testing of the web application.

claim: Predictions were calculated in less than 2 s for datasets up to 2000 patients.
source: In all cases, predictions were calculated in less than 2 s for datasets up to 2000 patients (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on performance testing of the web application.

claim: The Data Protection Office of the Max Planck Society assisted in assuring the legal fit of the web application to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
source: Further, the Data Protection Office of the Max Planck Society assisted in assuring the legal fit of the web application to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
evidence: This claim describes the legal compliance process.

claim: Forty-two hospitals from three Latin American countries provided data for external evaluation between March 7th 2020 to October 16th 2021.
source: To make a stringent external evaluation of this application with datasets collected from very different patient cohorts, we established a multinational collaboration with 42 hospitals from three Latin American countries (Figure 4A), which at the time of this evaluation were under a new surge of COVID-19 infections and admissions coinciding with the beginning of the Autumn-Winter season in the Southern Hemisphere. All these hospitals provided the values for the 12 features used by CODOP and measured in patients at the time of hospitalization between March 7th 2020 to October 16th 2021.
evidence: This claim describes the external validation cohorts.

claim: CODOP-Ovt achieved 78–100% sensitivity and 48–67% specificity in the Latin American validation cohorts.
source: A detailed analysis of the results indicates that if these were a prospective study, CODOP-Ovt would have identified the majority of the patients that finally died during hospitalization albeit wrongly classifying them as high-risk a significant number of patients that finally survived (78–100% sensitivity and 48–67% specificity, respectively; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the external validation results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CODOP-Unt achieved 89–97% specificity and 19%–50% sensitivity in the Latin American validation cohorts.
source: On the other side, the use of CODOP-Unt would have correctly triaged the vast majority of the survivors despite missing a significant number of patients that finally died (89–97% specificity and 19%–50% sensitivity, respectively; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the external validation results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The online version of CODOP could represent a useful clinical tool in the triage decision protocols.
source: These results strongly suggest that the online version of CODOP could represent a useful clinical tool in the triage decision protocols.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation results.

claim: CODOP satisfies the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis principles (TRIPOD).
source: CODOP satisfies the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis principles (Collins et al., 2015) (TRIPOD; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by adherence to reporting guidelines and citation.

claim: CODOP follows the recently proposed MINimum Information for Medical AI Reporting (MINIMAR).
source: follows the recently proposed MINimum Information for Medical AI Reporting (Hernandez-Boussard et al., 2020) (MINIMAR; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by adherence to reporting guidelines and citation.

claim: CODOP has been successfully checked for the risk of bias and applicability using the Prediction model study Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST).
source: and it has been successfully checked for the risk of bias and applicability using the Prediction model study Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (Moons et al., 2019) (PROBAST; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bias assessment and citation.

claim: Several machine learning-based prediction tools have been developed during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: In addition, several machine learning-based prediction tools have been developed during this pandemic.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the field.

claim: Independent validation studies have dismissed the clinical utility of all existing COVID-19 prediction models.
source: However, independent validation studies have dismissed the clinical utility of all these models (Wynants et al., 2020; El-Solh et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to validation studies.

claim: Common pitfalls of existing models include small sample size, use of variables not easily measurable in most hospitals, and lack of external evaluation datasets gathered in geographically different cohorts.
source: and have indicated common pitfalls to be avoided such as small sample size, use of variables not easily measurable in most hospitals, and lack of external evaluation datasets gathered in geographically different cohorts, etc.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited validation studies.

claim: The initial training and test cohorts encompassed 24,345 patients from more than 110 hospitals spread over Spain and the USA.
source: For this we used an initial training and test cohorts encompassing 24,345 patients from more than 110 hospitals spread over Spain and the USA and gathered during three pandemic waves.
evidence: This claim describes the size and composition of the training and test cohorts.

claim: The training and test cohorts were gathered during three pandemic waves.
source: For this we used an initial training and test cohorts encompassing 24,345 patients from more than 110 hospitals spread over Spain and the USA and gathered during three pandemic waves.
evidence: This claim describes the temporal coverage of the cohorts.

claim: The size, heterogeneity of the patient population, and the myriad of clinical and analytical procedures performed during the pandemic ensures a significant number of perturbations (shifts) in how the data were generated.
source: Both the size, heterogeneity of the patient population (in terms of age range, ethnicity, comorbidities, etc.), and the myriad of clinical and analytical procedures performed during the pandemic, ensures a significant number of perturbations (shifts) in how the data were generated.
evidence: This is an inference about the characteristics of the dataset.

claim: The inflammatory process underlying the clinical manifestations is similar in most of the hospitalized patients independently of their vaccination status or the type of VOC.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that the discriminative ability of CODOP is not hampered by the different immune protection status (either by infection or by vaccination) or by the type of VOC, which suggests that the inflammatory process underlying the clinical manifestations is similar in most of the hospitalized patients independently of their vaccination status or the type of VOC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stability of CODOP across different patient groups.

claim: The higher performance achieved by CODOP when compared to published mortality risk scores is due to the use of a group of biochemical parameters representing the main biological pathways involved in the pathogenesis of SARS-CoV-2.
source: In addition to the characteristics of our cohorts, we hypothesized that the higher performance achieved by CODOP when compared to published mortality risk scores is due to the use of a group of biochemical parameters representing the main biological pathways involved in the pathogenesis of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: A very common clinical manifestation in critical COVID-19 patients is composed of a deregulated immune response and a robust inflammatory reaction (known as 'hypercytokinemia' or 'cytokine storm'), which ultimately leads to tissue injury.
source: A very common clinical manifestation in critical COVID-19 patients is composed of a deregulated immune response and a robust inflammatory reaction (known as 'hypercytokinemia' or 'cytokine storm'), which ultimately leads to tissue injury (Chen and Quach, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Quach, 2021.

claim: Recent reports show a downregulated type-I interferon response leading to an increase of neutrophils in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Recent reports show a downregulated type-I interferon response leading to an increase of neutrophils in severe COVID-19 patients (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: The data show alterations in several myeloid cells (eosinophils, monocytes) including an upregulation in the number of neutrophils.
source: These findings go in line with our data showing alterations in several myeloid cells (eosinophils, monocytes) including an upregulation in the number of neutrophils (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claim: Myeloid cells are crucial for mounting a successful immune response against viruses and for the existence of hypercytokinemia.
source: Myeloid cells are crucial for mounting a successful immune response against viruses and for the existence of hypercytokinemia (Bordon et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bordon et al., 2013.

claim: The increased level of CRP and LDH could represent easy-to-measure hallmarks of the exacerbated inflammatory response associated with a high risk of COVID-19-related death.
source: The increased level of CRP and LDH in our dataset and their predictive value could represent easy-to-measure hallmarks of the exacerbated inflammatory response associated with a high risk of COVID-19-related death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Model features linked to thromboembolic complications (i.e. D-dimer and Platelets) and organ failure (i.e. Creatinine) could represent a warning signature easy to evaluate at early stages of the infection.
source: These and other model features linked to thromboembolic complications (i.e. D-dimer and Platelets) and organ failure (i.e. Creatinine), could represent a warning signature easy to evaluate at early stages of the infection, even before failure in major functions can be monitored.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: C-reactive Protein (CRP) is useful to recognize patients with an increased risk of mortality during hospitalization.
source: As example, C-reactive Protein (CRP) is useful to recognize patients with an increased risk of mortality during hospitalization (Stringer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stringer et al., 2021.

claim: The 12 parameter CODOP model has higher predictive performance than the CRP when analyzed as univariate.
source: However, the 12 parameter CODOP model has higher predictive performance than the CRP when analyzed as univariate (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the univariate analysis.

claim: The elevated price of Interleukin 6 or suPAR analysis precludes its widely use in Emergency Departments, particularly in low-income countries.
source: For other biomarkers (e.g. Interleukin 6 Coomes and Haghbayan, 2020 or suPAR Altintas et al., 2021), the elevated price of the analysis precludes its widely use in Emergency Departments, particularly in low-income countries.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about the cost of these biomarkers and is supported by citations.

claim: The advantage of a multi-parameter predictor like CODOP is based on its ability to represent the myriad of pathophysiological alterations occurring during the evolution of the COVID-19.
source: The advantage of a multi-parameter predictor like CODOP is based on its ability to represent the myriad of pathophysiological alterations (not only immune dysregulation) occurring during the evolution of the COVID-19 what might be the base for its good predictive capacity in a very diverse population.
evidence: This is an inference about why CODOP performs well.

claim: Six comorbidities were chosen together with the same 12 biochemical parameters in an alternative model.
source: Interestingly, while six comorbidities were chosen together with the same 12 biochemical parameters, their addition to CODOP did not improve its discriminative ability (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of comorbidities.

claim: The addition of six comorbidities to CODOP did not improve its discriminative ability.
source: Interestingly, while six comorbidities were chosen together with the same 12 biochemical parameters, their addition to CODOP did not improve its discriminative ability (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of comorbidities.

claim: CODOP excels in the 'Conceptual Reproducibility or Replicability' due to the use of geographically spread cohorts.
source: In comparison to previous studies, CODOP excels in the 'Conceptual Reproducibility or Replicability' due to the use of geographically spread cohorts (McDermott et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is an assessment of CODOP's reproducibility and is supported by citation.

claim: The use of training and test datasets with a high degree of perturbations adds several sources of variability including pre-analytical, analytical, intra- and inter-individual, and inter-hospital and geographical differences.
source: On the one side, the use of training and test datasets with a high degree of perturbations (see above) adds several sources of variability (Aarsand et al., 2019): pre-analytical due to differences in blood sampling, analytical due to different laboratory protocols, intra- and inter-individual, and inter-hospital and geographical differences in clinical practices.
evidence: This claim discusses limitations and is supported by citation.

claim: The high diversity of COVID-19 encompassing more than 60 disease subtypes sets a limitation in terms of the discriminability ability and the overall clinical utility of any MHL.
source: As an additional factor, the high diversity of COVID-19 encompassing more than 60 disease subtypes (DeMerle et al., 2021) sets a limitation in terms of the discriminability ability and the overall clinical utility of any MHL.
evidence: This claim discusses limitations and is supported by citation.

claim: CODOP does not take into account the level of care received by each patient (e.g. ICU versus basic care).
source: In contrast to other predictors, CODOP does not take into account the level of care received by each patient (e.g. ICU versus basic care), which influences the outcome of the patient and perturbs the discrimination ability of CODOP (as predictions are made with the data from blood analyses at hospital admission).
evidence: This claim discusses a limitation of CODOP.

claim: The proposed objective of CODOP is not to indicate a specific clinical treatment or decision but rather to inform physicians about the monitoring needs of patients.
source: The proposed objective of CODOP is not to indicate a specific clinical treatment or decision (e.g. yes/no admission to ICU), but rather to inform physicians about the monitoring needs of patients (i.e. a higher death risk score suggests a closer monitorization of the patient).
evidence: This claim describes the intended use of CODOP.

claim: CODOP is less effective for predicting the admission of a patient to the ICU or the need for mechanical ventilation.
source: In this line, the analysis of a small court of patients (belonging to the Test 4 and the Argentinian COVID-19 Network cohorts) shows that CODOP is less effective for predicting the admission of a patient to the ICU or the need for mechanical ventilation (Supplementary file 1t).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ICU admission and mechanical ventilation prediction.

claim: CODOP could be an interesting tool to increase the number of expected critical events, therefore potentially reducing the sample size calculation.
source: Based on the ability of CODOP to stratify the severity of patients, CODOP could be an interesting tool to increase the number of expected critical events, therefore potentially reducing the sample size calculation.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential uses of CODOP.

claim: CODOP could be useful for the analysis of observational studies.
source: In the same line, CODOP could be useful for the analysis of observational studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential uses of CODOP.

claim: Future participation of more institutions from regions non-represented in the study (Africa, Asia) will improve the reproducibility and overall clinical utility of CODOP.
source: We expect that future participation of more institutions from regions non-represented in our study (Africa, Asia) will improve the reproducibility and overall clinical utility of CODOP supporting subgroup-specific predictions (e.g. based on underlying comorbidities or ethnical background).
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements to CODOP.

claim: The training cohort consisted of 15902 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in 109 Spanish healthcare centres during the first COVID-19 wave between February 5th and July 6th 2020.
source: We developed CODOP following a multistep process (Figure 1) using a training dataset with measurements of 20 features (18 blood biochemical parameters plus Age and Sex; Table 1) routinely measured during admission on 15902 COVID-19 patients hospitalized in 109 Spanish healthcare centres during the first COVID-19 wave that occurred in Spain between February 5th and July 6th 2020 (SEMI-COVID-19 Network database Casas-Rojo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim describes the training cohort and is supported by citation.

claim: The training dataset included measurements of 20 features (18 blood biochemical parameters plus Age and Sex).
source: using a training dataset with measurements of 20 features (18 blood biochemical parameters plus Age and Sex; Table 1)
evidence: This claim describes the features used in training.

claim: Data pre-processing included standardization of the laboratory tests units and imputation of the missing test values.
source: As a first step, data pre-processing included standardization of the laboratory tests units and imputation of the missing test values, which is characteristic of real-world clinical practice (Table 1).
evidence: This claim describes the data preprocessing steps.
